messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 42
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Combat Pilot
- Trauma Type: Relief worker in war zone
- Pcl5: 66

# Vignette: Major Anya Vreeland, Age 42

Anya has spent the better part of two decades in the cockpit. She is the kind of woman who describes turbulence as "interesting" and who once landed a damaged aircraft with a calm that made her ground crew go quiet. Precision is her language. Control is her religion. It is perhaps why what happened in the summer of her thirty-ninth year has taken such a thorough and merciless hold on her.

Three years ago, Anya was seconded to a humanitarian coordination mission in a conflict zone in Eastern Europe — not flying combat sorties, but ferrying relief workers and medical supplies into areas that had been negotiated into temporary ceasefires. She had done similar work before. She believed in it. On the fourth week of the mission, she was on the ground helping to offload medical equipment when a shell struck a makeshift distribution center two hundred meters away. She ran toward it because that is who she is. What she found there — a collapsed structure, children who had been waiting for food parcels, a young aid worker she had flown in herself that morning — is something she has not yet been able to describe in full to anyone, including her husband, Pieter.

She completed the mission. She flew home. She told Pieter it had been difficult and then did not speak of it again for nearly eight months.

What began as sleeplessness gradually became something more architectural. Anya now wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, her heart pounding as though she is pulling out of a steep dive. The dreams are not always literal replays — sometimes it is just smoke, and a particular quality of silence, and the knowledge that she is too late. She lies in the dark beside Pieter and does not wake him, because she has decided, in the private logic of her suffering, that her distress is a failure of discipline.

In the cockpit, she remains technically proficient — her commanding officer has noticed nothing. But she has begun to hate flying over open ground at low altitude. A certain angle of afternoon light, the kind that turns dust golden, can send her somewhere she doesn't want to go. She has learned to manage these moments with a clenched jaw and a tight focus on her instruments. She has not told her flight surgeon.

At home, she has become careful in ways that exhaust her. She avoids the news. She has stopped watching films with any violence, which once would have struck her as absurd — she used to enjoy war films, could discuss their tactical inaccuracies with cheerful authority. Now she leaves the room. She has grown quieter at dinner, and Pieter, a patient and perceptive man, has begun to ask questions she deflects with competence. She loves him and cannot reach him. This frightens her more than she admits.

She carries a persistent and grinding guilt about the aid worker — a twenty-six-year-old named Sofie — that has calcified into something close to a belief: that she should have known, that she should have seen something, that a pilot of her experience does not make the kind of judgment that puts someone in the wrong place. The logic is airtight only in the way that grief logic is airtight — circular, self-sealing, immune to argument.

She has begun to wonder whether she is the person she thought she was. The woman who landed the damaged aircraft trusted herself completely. Anya is no longer sure she has access to that woman. She describes herself, in one of her rare moments of candor, as feeling like she is flying with instruments she can no longer fully read — aware that she is airborne, uncertain of her altitude, watching the gauges and waiting for something to confirm what she already fears.
